analysis.one_liner: Lets shooting victims sue gun makers and dealers by repealing the industry's federal lawsuit shield.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 141 cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2005, a federal law called the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act has blocked most lawsuits against gun makers, sellers, and dealers for harms caused when a gun is criminally misused. No other consumer product has this protection — car makers, drug companies, and toy manufacturers can all be sued. This bill would repeal that shield, so someone injured or who lost a family member to gun violence could sue the manufacturer or dealer the way victims of other products can. It would also unlock ATF gun trace data so plaintiffs' lawyers could use it as evidence to show which dealers supplied crime guns. The bill never received a hearing or vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured or bereaved by gun violence gain the ability to sue gun manufacturers, sellers, and dealers in negligence and product-liability cases, as victims of other consumer products already can. Their lawyers gain access to ATF trace data as evidence, which can reveal which dealers supplied the guns used in shootings. Communities that have used litigation to push dealers toward safer sales practices gain the same tool.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, the 2005 law that blocks most civil suits against gun manufacturers, sellers, and dealers for harms caused by criminal or unlawful use of a firearm.

Allows victims and their families to sue the gun industry under the same negligence and product-liability rules that apply to car makers, pharmaceutical companies, and other consumer products, giving them a path to compensation and to court-ordered changes in industry behavior.

Makes the ATF's firearms trace database discoverable and admissible as evidence in civil and administrative proceedings, so plaintiffs can identify which dealers and distributors supplied guns used in crimes instead of facing a legal wall around that data.

analysis.who_pays: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and their trade association would face civil lawsuits and potentially large verdicts for negligent sales or distribution, plus the litigation costs of discovery into their sales records and the newly opened ATF trace data. Gun prices and insurance costs for dealers could rise as a result.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations

drawbacks.text: The current liability shield exists because guns are legal products whose misuse is a criminal act by a third party; without it, manufacturers and lawful dealers could face massive jury verdicts for actions of criminals they never dealt with, which industry supporters argue could bankrupt some manufacturers and disrupt lawful sales.

Opening the ATF firearms trace database to full discovery would expose sensitive law-enforcement information in litigation, and some officials have long argued that could compromise ongoing investigations, witnesses, and officer safety.

Even with the shield repealed, suits must still prove negligence or a specific legal claim; repeal creates access to the courts, not automatic liability, so the practical effect for any individual case would depend on the facts and state law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and significant: repeal would give shooting victims and their families the same access to the courts that victims of other unsafe products have, and trace data access could expose negligent dealers. The cost is that firearms, unlike most products, are intentionally dangerous when misused, so the threat of large jury verdicts could push manufacturers to raise prices, reduce dealer networks, or exit segments of the market — which is exactly the argument the industry makes and exactly the pressure mechanism supporters intend. Whether that pressure deters negligent distribution or also punishes fully lawful commerce is a genuine design question the bill never got to be debated on.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress; the committee never voted on it and the full House never saw it.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced H.R. 4184 on June 15, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which is the only action the bill ever received.
The bill attracted 141 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat, giving it solid support on paper but no path to a floor vote in a chamber where majority-party support was absent.

The House Judiciary Committee, chaired by a Republican, never held a markup or vote on the bill, so it could not reach the House floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, when all unpassed bills expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations are better off, because the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act shield from civil lawsuits remains in force and unchallenged. Shooting victims and their families remain barred from most suits against the gun industry.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The gun industry, which keeps its lawsuit shield

for.name: Rep. Adam B. Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 15, 2023 with 50 original cosponsors.

for.name: 141 House cosponsors
for.role: Members of the House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors — all Democrats — supporting repeal of the gun industry's liability shield.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary (Chair Jim Jordan, R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 15, 2023 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee.

against.name: National Rifle Association and gun industry trade groups
against.what_they_did: Have long championed the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act as their top legislative priority and opposed every attempt to repeal it.

sides.party_line_note: All 141 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill had no Republican support on record, while the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee and House majority gave it no hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations
industries.note: The bill repeals the federal law that shields them from most civil suits over criminal misuse of their products, exposing them to the same litigation risk as other consumer industries. It also opens ATF trace data to discovery, making it easier to trace crime guns back to specific dealers. For ordinary people, that litigation channel is the point: it is the main way victims could obtain compensation and force changes in how guns are sold.

industries.industry: Victims of gun violence and their families
industries.note: Not an industry, but the concentrated beneficiary: the bill restores their standing to sue for injuries and deaths caused by guns, a right removed for this product category in 2005.
